1:
Nearly the whole entry turns on the title and on the four words for sin. Matthew Henry allows that Maschil may be only the name of a tune, but prefers the margin, a psalm giving instruction, and says there is nothing in which we have more need of instruction than the nature of true blessedness. John Calvin rejects the derivation of the word from the promise to instruct later in the psalm and takes it as a title given in accordance with the whole scope and subject matter. Adam Clarke calls it instructive by way of eminence, supposes it composed after the transgression with Bath-sheba and after pardon was obtained, and reports that the Syriac heads it a psalm concerning the sin of Adam and a prophecy concerning Christ, while the Arabic makes it spoken prophetically concerning the redemption. Keil and Delitzsch couple it with the psalm before it, noting that both look back on some fact of the psalmist’s spiritual life and both close with an exhortation to the godly, and place it as the second of the seven penitential psalms of the church and the favourite of Augustine, whose saying that the first part of understanding is to know oneself a sinner they take as its motto; for a whole year after his adultery, they add, David was like a man under sentence of condemnation.

Adam Clarke counts four evils named here and three acts that remove them: transgression is the passing over a boundary, doing what is prohibited; sin is the missing of a mark, not doing what was commanded; iniquity is what is turned out of its proper course, anything morally distorted; guile is fraud and deceit — and against them stand forgiving, covering, and not imputing, the first meaning borne away, as by a vicarious sacrifice. John Gill reads the forgiveness the same way, as a lifting off and carrying away of a burden too heavy for the sinner to bear, the sin having first been transferred to Christ the surety as the sins of the people were put upon the scapegoat. C.H. Spurgeon observes that the psalm opens with beatitudes as the sermon on the mount does, and that where the first psalm pictures the tree in full growth this one shows its planting and watering: blessedness is here ascribed not to a diligent lawkeeper, for then it would never come to us, but to a lawbreaker forgiven, so that self-righteous Pharisees have no portion in it. Samson carried the gates of Gaza, he adds, but what was that to the weight Jesus bore.

John Calvin presses the blessedness into a doctrine: it utterly destroys the righteousness of works, and the threefold repetition is not vain but aimed two ways at once, to rouse those asleep under an immense load of sins and to steady the fearful whose doubts come one after another. He denies that pardon is needed only at the beginning of righteousness, since believers are every day involved in faults, and rejects as half a pardon the distinction between remitting the punishment and remitting the fault. Augustine of Hippo holds that not by the merits of works but by the grace of God is man delivered, confessing his sins, and takes the absence of guile to mean that a man has no boastings of righteousness in his mouth while his conscience is full of sins. Matthew Henry makes the same distinction sharply: the text does not say there is no guilt, for who lives and sins not, but no guile — the pardoned sinner does not repent with a purpose to sin again and then sin with a purpose to repent again. John Wesley puts it as freely confessing all his sins and turning from sin to God with all his heart.
3:
The silence is described from the inside and the voices differ only in pitch. John Gill takes it as being unthoughtful of sin and making no acknowledgment of it, quite senseless and stupid, and notes that the Targum adds the words from the law, pointing at sin as the cause of what follows. Adam Clarke says only that before he humbled himself his soul was under the deepest horror. John Wesley reads the silence as withholding a full and open confession, so that the spirit failed and the strength of the body decayed, the roaring coming from the continual horrors of conscience. Charles Ellicott agrees that the verse describes the state of mind before he could bring himself to confess, and sets beside it lines on a knight of story whose mood was often like a fiend and drove him into wastes and solitudes for agony, and whose remorseful pain had marred his face and marked it before his time. C.H. Spurgeon goes furthest: while we smother sin it rages within like a gathering wound, until the voice is no longer articulate speech but resembles the hoarse roaring of a wounded beast; the rack, the wheel and the flaming fagot are ease, he says, compared with what a guilty conscience kindles in the breast, and the Spanish inquisition with all its tortures was nothing to the inquest conscience holds within the heart.

The dried moisture divides them. John Gill takes the heavy hand as an affliction continuing night and day without intermission, and thinks it may design some violent distemper, perhaps a fever; John Wesley says simply that the moisture was dried up, and C.H. Spurgeon that if the finger of God can crush us, what must the hand be, pressing heavily and continuously. Charles Ellicott works instead on the word, which occurs only once elsewhere, where the Authorised Version gives fresh oil and the Septuagint and Vulgate an oily cake; here those two seem to have read something else altogether, turning the clause into being turned to sorrow while the thorn was fixed in, with Symmachus giving destruction for sorrow and Aquila spoiling in summer desolation — all of which, he says, mistake the letter that is part of the word for a preposition. Following Gesenius he connects it with an Arabic root meaning to suck, and so reaches juice or moisture; and against Gill he holds that the drought is better taken not of a literal fever but of the soul-fever the whole passage describes.

On the confession John Gill observes that the psalmist uses the same three words for sin here that were used in the doctrine of pardon above, his confession being of the same extent as the pardon, and that God is not informed of anything but the sinner expresses his own sense of what is ever before him. Adam Clarke gives it as a sequence of things felt — the hardness of heart, the deep distress, the power to confess and abhor, the confidence in mercy, and at last the forgiveness — and reads the pause that follows as an attestation: this is all true, I know it, I felt it, I feel it. Matthew Henry guards the point: repentance and confession do not merit the pardon of transgression, though they are needful to the real enjoyment of forgiving mercy, and it is very difficult to bring sinful man humbly to accept free mercy with full self-condemnation. Charles Ellicott alone will not read the verse as it stands, urging that both verbs are future and adopting the suggestion that the words I said have changed place and belong at the beginning.
6:
What the time of finding is divides the entry. Adam Clarke makes it a condition of the man rather than of the calendar: when the heart is softened and the conscience alarmed, that is a time of finding, for God is ever ready and men are not; who can pray with a hard heart and a dark mind? while you feel relentings, pray. C.H. Spurgeon reads it as a term that expires: between the time of sin and the day of punishment mercy rules the hour, but once the sentence has gone forth pleading is useless, and the ungodly postpone their petitions until the master of the house has risen up and shut the door. John Wesley keeps it to the season while God continues to offer grace and mercy. Charles Ellicott declines to fill the ellipsis with forgiveness at all: some general word such as goal or object is more probably wanted, and the ancient versions render it the appointed time and opportune. Keil and Delitzsch turn the verse into an exhortation — for this mercy, provided for every sinner who repents and confesses, let every godly man who longs for mercy turn in prayer at the time when God and his mercy are to be found.

Underneath that lies a sharper difference about what is being asked for. John Gill holds that God has by one eternal act forgiven all trespasses at once for the sake of Christ, so that no new act of pardon can arise in the mind of God, nor a fresh one pass in the court of heaven; the prayer of the godly must therefore be understood of praying for the manifestation of that pardon to their consciences. The others take the petition at face value as a request for the thing itself, Adam Clarke grounding it on the mercy already shown to all who have truly turned, and C.H. Spurgeon observing that remarkable answers quicken the prayerfulness of others: where one man finds a golden nugget others feel inclined to dig, and the case of David has led thousands to seek the Lord with hopeful courage who might otherwise have died in despair. On the floods that shall not come nigh, Adam Clarke reads violent trials, temptations and afflictions beating on a house founded on a rock; John Wesley a time of great calamities that shall not overwhelm; Charles Ellicott leaves open whether they figure divine judgment or trial.

The hiding place draws out the boldest image of the entry. Adam Clarke takes it as an allusion, probably, to the city of refuge: the avenger of blood shall not be able to overtake him, and being encompassed with an impregnable wall he knows himself safe. John Gill guards the promise, since the saints are not preserved from having trouble — in this world they must have tribulation and through it enter the kingdom — but from being swallowed up by it. Matthew Henry makes the safety turn on something else again: having tasted the sweetness of pardoning mercy to a penitent sinner he cannot doubt its continuance to a praying saint, and yet if God pardons our sins and then leaves us to ourselves we shall soon run as far in debt again as ever; God keeps his people from trouble by keeping them from sin. The songs of deliverance he will not keep private: his friends shall compass him about in the great congregation, so that as every one who is godly prays with him, they shall give thanks with him too.
8:
Who is speaking here is the question of the entry. C.H. Spurgeon answers flatly that the Lord is the speaker, giving the psalmist an answer to his prayer; Adam Clarke that these are probably the Lord’s words to David, promising all the assistance requisite now that he is sensible of the mercy received; John Wesley that David brings God in as returning this answer to his prayers; and John Gill that they are by many thought to be the words of the Lord, who instructs by his providence, even by afflictive dispensations, by his written word, by its ministers and by his Spirit. Keil and Delitzsch deny it outright: it is not God who speaks here, for the person addressed would then have to be the poet, who has already attained the knowledge in question; it is the poet himself who now adopts the tone of the teacher, taking in hand what he promises elsewhere, the instruction of sinners in the way of salvation. Charles Ellicott finds the change to the first person so abrupt that he prefers, with most of the old interpreters and with Ewald, Hitzig and Reuss among the moderns, to suppose them the words of deliverance sounding sweet in the psalmist’s ears.

On being guided with the eye Charles Ellicott allows two renderings, advising with the eye upon him or fixing the eye upon him, and prefers the second on the authority of the Septuagint. Adam Clarke makes it mutual — I will keep mine eyes upon thee, and thou shalt keep thine upon me. C.H. Spurgeon reads it as the discipline of a household: as servants take their cue from the master’s eye, and a nod or a wink is all they require, so we should obey the slightest hints, not needing thunderbolts to startle our incorrigible sluggishness but being controlled by whispers and love-touches; and he adds that we are not pardoned in order to live after our own lusts but to be educated in holiness, so that men who never sat at the feet of Gamaliel and know nothing of Aristotle are thrice happy if they have learned to follow the Lamb. John Wesley finds the look already given once, as it was given to Peter when the Lord turned and looked upon him. Matthew Henry adds only that God teaches by his word and guides by the secret intimations of his will.

The horse and the mule are read morally by most and textually by one. Adam Clarke presses the contrast — they act only by force and constraint, while a rational soul owes a reasonable service, and he warns against obliging our Maker to have continual recourse to afflictions and severe dispensations to keep us in the way. John Gill extends the figure into three faults: thoughtless and unteachable, or stubborn and untractable, stopping the ear and pulling away the shoulder, or downright mischievous, kicking and persecuting those who undertake to instruct them, as such creatures try to throw their riders and kick at them when they are down. John Wesley notes only that all the ancient translators take the clause of a compulsion by bit and bridle. Charles Ellicott reports that here the text has evidently suffered and the exact meaning is lost: the word rendered mouth elsewhere means ornament, so that the literal sense is with bit and bridle his ornament to hold, not approaching to thee, which may mean that the animal is harnessed so that it may not approach, or because without harness it will not; the Septuagint and Vulgate give jaws instead, and Ewald follows them.
10:
The sorrows of the wicked are read at different depths. John Gill takes them outwardly and inwardly at once — consuming diseases brought on by intemperance, families reduced to a piece of bread, and then the remorse that seizes the conscience when it is at last open to conviction; and he concedes that wicked men for the most part have their good things in this life, only what they have is with a curse and carries no true peace. Adam Clarke compresses it into a marriage: God has wedded sin and misery as strongly as he has wedded holiness and happiness, and none can put them asunder. John Wesley notes only that the sorrows are an argument to enforce the admonition just given. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the animals of the previous verse in view — like refractory horses and mules they have many cuts and bruises — and sets the two states side by side in an image of his own: the wicked have a hive of wasps around them, but the trusting have a swarm of bees storing honey for them.

On the closing call to be glad C.H. Spurgeon makes joy a duty rather than a permission, since God has made it part of our obedience to be joyful and rebellious murmuring is therefore sinful. John Gill follows the Targum, which reads it as gladness in the Word of the Lord, and takes that of Christ the essential Word, the righteousness imputed to them by which they become righteous. Adam Clarke grants that man was made for happiness but insists the happiness be founded on holiness, which comes from God and is retained only by continual union with him — and then adds, alone among them, that this verse probably belongs to the psalm following and was originally its first. Keil and Delitzsch read it the other way, as the deliberate close of this psalm: after the doctrine has been unfolded in three unequal groups of verses there follows, answering to the brief introduction, a still shorter ending that calls those whose happy state has been celebrated to join in songs of exultant joy.
